- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

1	# Junior delegation protocol
2	
3	The full protocol referenced from `SKILL.md`'s "Gates worth remembering" section — decided from the
4	request, BEFORE the first tool call (SPEC INV-69).
5	
6	**Junior delegation (decided from the request, BEFORE the first tool call):** the trigger is judgment
7	against mechanical — work whose steps can be written precisely (known edit strings, a known command,
8	fan-out fact-gathering, a report or list or dump to produce) routes to a worker, while anything carrying
9	judgment or design stays senior. Size is a weak hint only, never the decider. The trigger, the tier
10	ladder, and the raw-output law all live in the base skill's rule 5 and the routing rule — this passage is
11	their reference; it is not a second home (live-spec-base rule 5, SPEC INV-69).
12	
13	**The routing rule (SPEC INV-69) picks the tier — propose the cheapest tier that can pass the brief, the
14	senior may overrule it aloud:** the proposal reads the STEP and kind of the work, beyond the row's size
15	alone — a judgment step (spec, prove, architecture, matrix-level calls, findings triage, any taste call)
16	proposes the senior and is never routed down, a mechanical step proposes a worker at the tier above. The
17	economy rung moves the threshold (at `lean` an airtight brief rides one tier cheaper, at `tight` the
18	cheapest sufficient tier is always the proposal). And the proposal is ADVISORY — the senior may override
19	per wish, the override logged as one line on the checkpoint and the delivery report, proposed tier → chosen
20	tier → why.
21	
22	**The brief is self-contained (the BMAD story-file lesson):** delegated work ships as one document
23	embedding the EXACT spec sentences it serves, the exact edit strings or commands, the checks to run, and
24	the checkpoint path — the worker never hunts context, never interprets the spec, never decides. If writing
25	the brief means deciding something first, that decision is the senior's and happens BEFORE delegation —
26	"explaining it would take longer than doing it" is how delegation silently dies.
27	
28	**The brief's birth has three laws (SPEC INV-53/54/55):** a brief that edits existing files is born from
29	READING them in full — three recorded lines per file (current state · what changes · what must survive),
30	every step back-referencing its spec sentence, every technical claim citing a source (a file:line, a
31	command's output), never memory of a file. The brief carries the closed HALT list — ambiguous requirement
32	· two consecutive unexplained failures of one command · missing config/dependency · acceptance impossible
33	as briefed — stop WITH evidence, otherwise run to completion (the senior's escalation ladder is a separate
34	move, after a failed acceptance). And the brief is SIZED — its text within ~300 lines, at most ~8 files to
35	edit [default], the work splitting above either — passing PATHS, never inlined file bodies. See the private
36	playbook repo's PLAYBOOK.md.
37	
38	**The worker contract (SPEC ACT-3):** the brief NAMES the files the worker may write — its session's
39	write-ownership narrowed to exactly those, reads free, writes fenced. Same-session sibling-worker files
40	are fence-benign (the concurrent-edit fence alarms on foreign sessions, staying quiet on your own briefed
41	hands — the senior who briefed both owns the seams between briefs). Owning those seams is a brief-time
42	act: before spawning another concurrent writer, the senior confirms its brief's write-set is disjoint
43	from every already-running writer's brief, or gives it an isolated worktree (SPEC INV-105) — because
44	the fence stays silent between same-session siblings, this disjointness is settled when the briefs are
45	written, ahead of the new worker's first write. The session's live setting lines ride
46	into the brief verbatim — a worker never resolves the settings ladder itself, it cannot hear the human's
47	spoken word.
48	
49	**A worker never restores a working tree with a git command (SPEC INV-298; the gate INV-299).** Before a worker
50	mutates a file it means to put back, it reads that file and holds its bytes. A worker puts a file
51	back by WRITING ITS OWN SAVED BYTES. A worker runs no command that discards uncommitted work, in any
52	tree: `git checkout -- <path>`, `git checkout .`, `git restore` outside `--staged`, `git stash` and
53	its `push`, `save`, `create` and `store` forms, `git reset` with `--hard`, `--merge` or `--keep`, and
54	`git clean` with `-f` or `-x`. Such a command's blast radius is a PATH, so its damage lands on files
55	the worker never wrote and its brief never named. This rule binds a worker in every tree, including
56	its own isolated worktree, since a worktree shares one repository with the lanes beside it and a
57	worker cannot read off its brief what else that repository holds. A worker that holds no saved bytes
58	for a file it mutated, or that believes a file needs a git-level restore, HALTS and reports the file
59	and the mutation it made, and it writes no further file and runs no further command. The
60	orchestrator owns recovery: it restores the named file from the last committed stage, hands the
61	worker a fresh brief carrying that file's current bytes, and records the halt in the row's delivery
62	report, and the halted work resumes under that new brief. The orchestrator's own half: a finished
63	build stage is committed before the next worker touches its files, so a worker that hits a broken
64	file has a commit to be recovered from. `guardrails/check-worker-restore.py` reads the worker runs'
65	transcripts for the command and runs at the verify step. The write-set disjointness above fences
66	EDITS and gives no cover here, which is why the clause stands on its own: the two destructions of
67	uncommitted work on 2026-07-23 and the near miss of 2026-07-27 all came from a worker running
68	correct-looking work, and the `git status` it pasted afterwards read "clean" in the safe case and the
69	destructive one alike. The clause rides every brief this protocol composes.
70	
71	**The brief carries the register laws, so the worker's own text obeys them (SPEC INV-221, INV-173).** The
72	brief states the register laws the worker's report and any agent-to-agent message must hold — the
73	no-scissors law (no naming a thing by denying its neighbour, SPEC INV-173) and the no-dramatization law
74	(grading the size of a change, up or down, is the reader's act, SPEC INV-221). A worker writes text a
75	human reads, and the chat and document judges [INV-203] never read its report, so the brief is where the
76	laws reach it. The worked instance: workers reporting to this pack opened "Excellent work" and named a
77	premise wrong "in an important way", both graded-size sentences the worker had no brief telling it to
78	drop (the owner's count, 2026-07-17).
79	
80	The brief ARMS the worker for the workshop — it carries the host's problem-ledger path
81	(`.live-spec/PROBLEMS.md`) with the WATCHED-line duty: workshop noise the worker hits (a flaky harness, a
82	missing dependency, a tool misbehaving) goes into its checkpoint as a ledger line — signature, date, one
83	line of context, logged every time — and the senior carries the lines into the ledger at verify (SPEC
84	INV-23). And it carries the CLOCK — the date and time read at briefing — so the worker stamps its
85	checkpoint and any dated output from the brief's clock, never an invented hour (SPEC INV-24; a worker WITH
86	a shell re-reads the machine clock itself — the brief's line is the floor for one without, and elapsed
87	time is never guessed). And a result failing its brief's acceptance escalates exactly ONE tier every time,
88	with a logged line covering the move — one rung up, in order, always logged.
89	
90	**Every delegation reports its saving:** the
91	delivery report carries one line — what went to the worker and roughly how much senior work it saved.
92	The line is what keeps the habit alive; a session that never writes it is a session that quietly
93	stopped delegating. The line lives in the row's delivery report, which the closing commit moves to the archive with the
94	row, and a suite check reads it from the archive: a delivered row without the line goes red
95	(SPEC INV-103, INV-276, forward from 2026-07-12).
96	 The same accounting also names the reads dispatched beside the work delegated, so a session that filled its own context with a read it should have dispatched shows that in the report (SPEC INV-137). Each work block in the report opens by naming its root, and the report accounts the block against its announced plan line (SPEC INV-314). The duty binds the
97	orchestrator seat regardless of model, whatever tier leads the seat.

3	description: Use to run a non-trivial feature, bug fix, behavior change, refactor, docs-only change, or feature removal through the full spec-to-ship pipeline. Use it as well to set a project up on live-spec, where it reads the tree, picks the setup walk, and runs it. 7	
8	# build-pipeline — ship a change by the method
9	
10	> Part of the **live-spec pack** — the shared working rules (ask-never-guess · plain words, anchors trail ·
11	> one surface = one name · one home per fact · junior/senior split · checkpoints · the concurrent-edit
12	> fence · freshness · journal discipline · attic-never-delete · verify by deed · the human's gates · claims
13	> need primary sources · fix the class, sweep look-alikes · the door before code · prototype ≠ product) live ONCE in the pack's base skill, `live-spec-base` (v5.0.0), together with the
14	> settings ladder — this skill references them and elaborates only its own domain. Used standalone, this
15	> note is plain advice.
16	
17	## Words this skill uses
18	
19	**Where the paths point.** Two repositories are in play. A path naming `skills/`, `guardrails/`,
20	`scripts/`, `templates/`, or `tests/` sits in the live-spec pack's own repository,
21	`github.com/happysasha18/live-spec`. An install copies each skill folder into one place, so a path
22	naming another skill points to that skill's folder, beside this skill's folder. A path opening with
23	`references/` names a file inside this skill's own directory, beside this file. Every other path
24	belongs to the project under change, including `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`,
25	`TEST_MATRIX.md`, `ROADMAP.md`, `JOURNAL.md`, `docs/prover/`, and `.live-spec/`.
26	
27	- **the pack** — the shipped live-spec method: its skills, its document templates, and its gates.
28	  `skills/live-spec-base/SKILL.md` holds the shared rulebook and names the ten working skills.
29	- **host** — one project the pack attaches to. Each host holds its own spec, queue, journal, and
30	  `.live-spec/` folder.
31	- **the human** — the person who owns the product decisions. A taste call, a threshold, and a policy
32	  all reach them.
33	- **seat** — the orchestrating session that owns judgment, briefs workers, and reports to the human.
34	  This page also calls that actor the senior and the orchestrator.
35	- **worker** — a delegated session the seat briefs for bounded mechanical work, narrowed to the files
36	  its brief names. This page also calls it the junior.
37	- **wish** — one request as it was spoken, before the door places it.
38	- **door** — the intake classification that places a wish at one entry point: feature, bug, refactor,
39	  docs-only, or skip. It is decided before any code is written, and it stands apart from the wish's size.
40	- **work-kind** — the intake axis naming what a wish produces: product, infra, skill, or prose.
41	- **footprint** — the reach of one change: presentation-only, single-module, or cross-cutting.
42	- **tripwire** — one fixed rule in the door step that lifts a wish to a door whatever its casual label.
43	- **row** — one line of the project's queue, `ROADMAP.md` in this pack, holding one piece of work.
44	- **spec-delta**, also **the delta** — the set of spec sentences one wish adds or changes.
45	- **regression fence** — one sentence in a delta naming a neighbouring promise that must stay true,
46	  citing the existing clause it guards.
47	- **landing** — the act of one piece of work reaching the repository's shared truth as one commit.
48	- **lane**, also **train** — one build lane a session rolls through the pipeline.
49	- **the pen** — the single write-lock a repository holds. One lane at a time writes shared files under it.
50	- **departures board** — the status view read live off the queue's open rows. It names each rolling
51	  lane's step, and whom a waiting lane waits behind.
52	- **red**, used as a verb — a check fails and stops the work at that point. **Green** names a run with
53	  zero failures.
54	- **gate** — a check that must pass before the work proceeds.
55	- **architecture node** — one named unit in `ARCHITECTURE.md`. It carries one responsibility, owns the
56	  spec facts it implements, and pins them to the code.
57	- **seam** — the named boundary between two nodes, stating what crosses it and who owns the format.
58	- **checkpoint** — a saved point of work a session or a worker resumes from, written under `.live-spec/`.
59	- **norm** — an approved prototype frozen as the binding record of a surface's look and feel, kept
60	  under `docs/norms/`.
61	- **problem ledger** — the per-host file `.live-spec/PROBLEMS.md`, recording the workshop's recurring
62	  operational noise.
63	- **class hunt** — the search a confirmed bug drives before it closes. Name the defect abstractly,
64	  find every sibling of that kind, and fix them together.
65	- **compaction** — the station that removes redundancy from a document or from code.
66	- **shopfront** — the public README as the reader-facing front of a repository.
67	- **attic** — the host's append-only archive folder, `attic/`, where a superseded file moves.
68	
69	**The bracket codes.** `INV-`, `T-`, `E-`, `ACT-`, and `M-` codes index requirements in this pack's
70	own `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`. `PRODUCT_SPEC.index.md` maps each code to the criteria that carry it. The word
71	`SPEC` before a code marks that same home and names no separate series. `M-1` is the milestone gate
72	and `M-6` is the push gate. A **base rule N** points at the numbered rule N in
73	`skills/live-spec-base/SKILL.md`; its own frontmatter states how many it carries. A **communicator rule N** points into
74	`skills/communicator/SKILL.md`. That file numbers twice: its behaviour rules carry an inline
75	`(rule N)` tag, and its writing-register checklist restarts at 1. This page names which of the two
76	it means each time.
77	Each sentence beside a code states its own
78	rule in full, so a reader holding this page alone can pass the codes over.
79	
80	## The pipeline in one line
81	
82	One pipeline, and steps 1, 2, 5, and 6 each invoke a named skill. The order is **spec → prove → architecture → prove architecture →
83	matrix → test → code → verify → commit & show**. A bug shortcuts to **bug → matrix → test → code** (citing the
84	existing architecture node it lands in). **Skip the pipeline only if ALL hold:** single
85	file · no new state / element / user-visible behaviour · an existing test level already covers the touched
86	fact (still ship a test; the order of test and fix follows test-author's small-fix path — red first by
87	default, and a one-batch fix owes the mechanical red proof). A skip still owes the door step's spec-backed-literal tripwire: does this edit touch a spec-backed literal or clause? A yes routes the docs and the test into the same session as the fix (SPEC INV-104). Anything touching visibility / layout / colour enters at the matrix step minimum.
88	Otherwise don't skip a step — the bugs that pass every test hide in the steps you skipped. (The private playbook repo's PLAYBOOK.md holds
89	the principle behind each step. This skill is its executable projection; keep the two in sync.)
90	
91	**The craft ladder — which craft's standards judge each step (SPEC INV-33).** Each artifact is judged by its
92	own craft's standards: **spec** — a strong product manager (the user's journey, the
93	product's words) · **prove / prove architecture** — the prover's formal-methods reviewer ·
94	**architecture** — a software architect (nodes, seams, one responsibility each) · **matrix** — a QA
95	automation lead deriving coverage · **test** — the same QA engineer writing it · **code** — a senior
96	developer · **verify** — the visitor's own fresh eyes, the builder's own view set aside · **commit & show** — a careful
97	release hand whose reader is the human.
98	
99	The delivery report's step accounting speaks in these standards. The craft each artifact was made under is
100	namable on ask.
101	
102	The craft takes the work-KIND's form (SPEC INV-22, INV-33): on a prose product the code step is worked as
103	a strong writer, on infra as a toolsmith. The ladder names the archetypes, and the kind says what their
104	standards look like in its medium.
105	
106	## When to run it — and where each kind of change enters
107	- **Step zero, before ANY tool call: name the door aloud (SPEC T-12, INV-16; base rule 15) — and the human hears the intake line back as the capture echo: heard · door · name · row · place on the map (communicator rule 12, its capture-echo behaviour rule; SPEC INV-27, INV-37).**
108	  - The intake line states size (a wish too big for its worth is negotiated in SCOPE — cut surfaces or
109	    split into stages, never a time budget or estimate; proposals proceed on the recommended option and
110	    are surfaced, SPEC T-15) · priority · door: feature · bug · refactor · docs-only · skip · work-kind: product · infra · skill ·
111	    prose — what the wish BUILDS, one kind per wish, scaling the FORM of every step it walks (the
112	    work-kind table at [references/work-kind-table.md](references/work-kind-table.md); SPEC T-16, INV-22).
113	
114	    The same line PLACES the wish on the product's feature map — **changes feature X · a new feature ·
115	    restructure** — spoken in the echo and written in the row's `map:` note. The map is the spec's scenario
116	    sections plus the architecture's nodes, never a third document. A restructure verdict queues its OWN row
